title: Beautiful Pairs
directAnswer: Count how many values A and B share as multisets — that is `Σ min(countA[v], countB[v])`, the maximum number of disjoint equal-value pairs. You must then change EXACTLY one element of B. If the multiset match already covers all n elements (every B element is paired), changing one element necessarily breaks a pair, so the answer is `matches − 1`. Otherwise there is an unmatched A value and a spare B element to retarget at it, giving `matches + 1`. O(n) with a hash map.

remember.pattern: Greedy multiset matching by value, then a forced ±1 from the mandatory single change
remember.formula:
matches = Σ over values v of min(countA[v], countB[v])
if matches == n: return matches - 1   # everything paired, a change must break one
else:            return matches + 1   # spare B element retargets an unmatched A value
rules: A 'beautiful pair' is a pairing of distinct indices (i, j) with `A[i] == B[j]`; each index of A and each index of B is used at most once.
The maximum disjoint matching equals the multiset intersection size `Σ min(countA[v], countB[v])` — never more, because each shared value v can back at most `min(countA[v], countB[v])` pairs.
You must change **exactly one** element of B — it is not optional. This is the whole twist of the problem.
If `matches < n` you can always do `matches + 1`: some A value is unmatched and some B element is unused, so retarget that B element to the A value.
If `matches == n` every B element is already paired, so any change destroys a pair and the best you can reach is `matches − 1` (then a re-pair recovers nothing because all were already used).
whenToUse: Maximising equal-value pairings between two collections where each element is consumed once
A multiset-intersection count is the core quantity
A constraint forces exactly one mutation and you must reason about its marginal effect
Pair counts are bounded by per-value minimum counts
antiSignals: Pairs are defined by an inequality or distance, not exact equality → sorting / two pointers, not counting
Elements may be reused across multiple pairs → not a disjoint matching
You may change any number of elements → the ±1 edge logic disappears
Order/positions matter (i must relate to j) → this is a different, positional problem
remember.takeaway: Maximum equal-value matching between two multisets is just `Σ min(countA[v], countB[v])` — counting beats searching. The interview spice is the mandatory single edit: reason about whether that edit can ADD a pair (slack exists) or is forced to REMOVE one (already saturated).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise the max matching as a multiset-intersection count, and whether you correctly handle the mandatory single change — especially the saturated case where the forced edit costs you a pair.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting the change is mandatory and just returning `matches`, or always returning `matches + 1` even when every element is already paired (which actually forces `matches − 1`).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Prove the cap: each value v contributes at most `min(countA[v], countB[v])` pairs, so the greedy count is optimal. Then case-split on whether slack exists for the forced edit.

problemStatement:
You are given two arrays, `A` and `B`, each containing `n` integers.

A pair of indices `(i, j)` is **beautiful** if `A[i] == B[j]`. A set of beautiful pairs is valid only if no index of `A` and no index of `B` is used more than once (a disjoint matching).

You must change **exactly one** element of `B` to any integer value. After making that single change, return the **maximum** possible number of beautiful pairs.
constraints: Exactly one element of B must be changed (the change is mandatory, not optional)
understanding: Without the edit, the most pairs you can form is the multiset overlap of A and B: for each value, you can pair it as many times as it appears in BOTH arrays. The edit is forced: you have to alter one B element. If the arrays aren't already fully paired, spend the edit to create a brand-new pair (+1). If they ARE fully paired, the edit can only damage an existing pair, dropping you to one less.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is changing an element of B optional or mandatory?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Mandatory — exactly one element of B must change. This is the crux: if everything is already matched, the change forces a loss.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the same value pair multiple times?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, but as a disjoint matching: value v can form min(countA[v], countB[v]) pairs, because each occurrence is consumed once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do the indices i and j have to be equal or related?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — any i can pair with any j as long as A[i] == B[j] and neither index is reused. Position is irrelevant.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What value can I change a B element to?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any integer. So if an A value is currently unmatched, you can always set a spare B element to exactly that value.

examples.explanation: Base matches: 1,2,3 pair up → 3 pairs (one extra B=3 is unused, A=4 unmatched). Not saturated, so change a spare B=3 into 4: B becomes [1,2,3,4], all 4 pair. Answer 3 + 1 = 4.
All 3 pair already (saturated, matches = n = 3). The mandatory change turns one B=3 into something else, breaking a pair → 3 − 1 = 2.
Only the value 5 is shared → 1 base pair. Not saturated, so retarget an unused B element (3 or 1) to an unmatched A value (10 or 16): 1 + 1 = 2.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Every Single Edit
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to show you respect the 'exactly one change' rule literally, then collapse it with counting.
hints: The rule says change exactly one element of B. The most literal plan is to try every possible single change and measure the result.
For each position j in B and each candidate value v (1..V), build the modified B and count the maximum disjoint equal-value matching.
Counting one matching is O(n) with a hash map; doing it for every (j, v) is O(n · V) builds × O(n) each → far too slow, but it makes the answer concrete.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n positions × V candidate values = n·V modified arrays, and scoring each matching is O(n). The product is O(n²·V) — only a teaching device.
approaches.explanation:
Take the rule at face value: you must change exactly one element of `B`. So enumerate every way to do that — pick a position `j` and a new value `v` — and for each resulting array compute the maximum number of beautiful pairs.

**How to score one array.** The maximum disjoint matching between two multisets is the intersection count: tally `B`'s values in a hash map, then walk `A` and consume one matching count per element that is still available. That single count is O(n).

**Why it's correct but wasteful.** Every legal single edit is examined, so the maximum over all of them is exactly the answer. But the candidate-value range `V` and the n positions multiply with the O(n) scoring, giving O(n²·V). For n, V up to 1000 that's a billion operations.

**The structure it exposes.** Scanning the results, two facts pop out. (1) The best you can ever reach is bounded by the base intersection count plus one — a single edit can create at most one new pair. (2) Whether you actually gain that `+1` depends only on whether the base matching already used every element. That collapses the whole search into one count and a case-split.
approaches.insight: Brute force reveals the answer is always within ±1 of the base intersection count, and which side you land on depends solely on saturation — turning an O(n²·V) search into an O(n) count.

approaches.name: Greedy — Multiset Intersection Count, Then Forced ±1 (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'count the shared values, then reason about the one mandatory edit'.
hints: Forget the edit for a moment. What is the maximum number of disjoint equal-value pairs between A and B? It is fixed by how many of each value the two arrays share.
For each value v, you can form min(countA[v], countB[v]) pairs. Sum that over all values to get the base matching.

Now bring back the mandatory edit. If the base matching used every element (matches == n), the edit must break a pair → matches − 1. Otherwise a spare B element can be retargeted to an unmatched A value → matches + 1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to count B (or A), one pass to consume matches against the other — O(n) time, O(n) for the hash map. The ±1 decision is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Tally one array's values in a hash map, then walk the other array consuming one available count per matching element. That sum is the base matching `matches = Σ min(countA[v], countB[v])`. Finally apply the mandatory edit with a one-line case-split.

**Why the count is the maximum — the exchange/upper-bound argument.** Consider any valid disjoint matching. Group its pairs by their shared value `v`. Each pair on value `v` consumes one occurrence of `v` from A and one from B, so the number of `v`-pairs cannot exceed `min(countA[v], countB[v])`. Summing this ceiling over all values gives an upper bound, and the greedy 'consume while available' construction *achieves* it for every value simultaneously (the values don't compete — a pair on value v never blocks a pair on a different value). Bound met = optimal.

**Why the forced edit gives +1 when there is slack.** If `matches < n`, then after the base matching at least one A index is unpaired (its value had no remaining B partner) and at least one B index is unused. Set that spare B element equal to the unmatched A value: a brand-new pair appears, and no existing pair is touched. So we reach `matches + 1`, and we cannot do better — one edit creates at most one new pair.

**Why the forced edit gives −1 when saturated.** If `matches == n`, every B element is already part of a pair. The mandatory change rewrites one of them; whatever new value it takes, the pair it used to serve is destroyed and at most that one pair can be re-formed elsewhere — but every other element is already consumed, so nothing is free to re-pair with it. The net is one fewer pair: `matches − 1`.
approaches.insight: Two independent ideas compose cleanly: (1) max equal-value matching = multiset intersection = `Σ min(countA, countB)`, provable by a per-value capacity argument; (2) a single mandatory edit shifts the answer by exactly +1 (if slack) or −1 (if saturated). Recognising 'matching capped by per-key minimum' is the reusable greedy kernel.

pitfalls: Returning `matches` and forgetting the change is mandatory.
Always returning `matches + 1` even when saturated — the saturated case is actually `matches − 1`.
Counting plain set intersection instead of multiset (min of counts) — drops valid duplicate pairs.

commonMistakes: Treating the single change as optional and returning the base matching.
Returning matches + 1 unconditionally, ignoring the saturated case that forces matches − 1.
Using set intersection instead of multiset min-count, undercounting duplicate-value pairs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ignoring the mandatory edit in the saturated case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When matches == n every element is already paired; a forced change must break a pair, so the answer is matches − 1, not matches or matches + 1.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
matches = sum(min(ca[v], cb[v]) for v in ca)
return matches + 1
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
matches = sum(min(ca[v], cb[v]) for v in ca)
return matches - 1 if matches == len(A) else matches + 1

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Set intersection instead of multiset
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Using distinct shared values drops duplicate pairings. A = [3,3], B = [3,3] should give 2 base pairs, not 1.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Python truthiness on a zero count
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Counter returns 0 for missing keys; `if count[b]:` is fine, but `if count.get(b):` with a defaultless dict would KeyError, and writing `if count[b] is not None` is wrong since 0 is a real value. Use `count[b] > 0`.

patternNote: Multiset-intersection matching capped by per-value min counts, plus a forced single-edit ±1 case-split. Recognise it whenever maximum equal-value pairings between two collections is the core, and a mandatory mutation perturbs the answer by exactly one.
